442.title: Beha'alotcha: a second Passover (Numbers 9:6–14)
442.hook: people who missed Passover ask for a chance, and one is given
442.howItsDone: Pesach Sheni falls on the fourteenth of Iyar, a month after Passover; with no Temple offering today, some Jews mark it by eating some matzah, and some communities omit penitential prayers that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron held the light to each wick until it rose alone. Your line was until it rises alone.

A group of people walk up to Moses with a complaint that sounds almost like a lawsuit. Everyone else is getting ready to keep Passover in the wilderness, a year after leaving Egypt. The lambs are chosen; the fires are being built. And these people can't take part. It's not their fault: they're ritually impure, because they've been near a dead body. Somebody had to handle the dead. Why, they ask, should we be left out? Moses doesn't give them an answer. He says: wait, and I'll ask.
screen: `EVERYONE IS READY FOR PASSOVER.` → `A GROUP LEFT OUT.` → `MOSES SAYS: WAIT.`

segments.voice: Numbers nine. The men say: we're impure from a dead body, "wherefore are we to be kept back," from bringing the LORD's offering at its time with everyone else? This law doesn't start as a command from above. It starts from below, with people who refuse to be shut out, and say so. God's answer creates a new date. Anyone impure from the dead, or far away on a journey, can keep Passover one month later, on the fourteenth of the second month, with matzah and bitter herbs. In Hebrew, Pesach Sheni: the second Passover. Who were they? The Talmud records a few opinions. One says they were carrying Joseph's coffin, the bones Moses brought out of Egypt. Another suggests they had buried someone who died with no one else to bury them. Either way, they were impure because they'd done something good. The Torah is honest about the edge of this, too. For someone who was clean, not on a journey, and simply didn't keep Passover, the verse has hard words: he shall bear his sin. The second date is for people life got in the way of. There's no Passover offering today, but the date is still marked. Some Jews eat a piece of matzah that day, a month after Passover. And in Chabad teaching it's often summed up in a simple line: it's never too late.

segments.voice: Think of someone who missed something with you, a birthday, a promise, a moment you needed them, and ask whether life got in the way of them, the way it did in the story. Hold that possibility gently, and picture offering a second date: let's try again, the door's open. You can offer yourself one too.
Pesach Sheni. The second Passover: one month later, for those who couldn't keep the first, given because they asked.
Your line: second chances exist. The door you missed can open again. Day four hundred forty-two, done.

443.title: Beha'alotcha: we remember the fish (Numbers 11:4–6)
443.hook: the people crave Egypt's fish and cucumbers, forgetting the whip
443.howItsDone: The people's craving for Egypt's food in Numbers 11 is read in Beha'alotcha each summer; Jewish teachers often use Rashi's reading of "for nought" to talk about how the memory of slavery can be softened into longing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesach Sheni, the second Passover for those who missed the first. Your line was second chances exist.

Someone runs into an ex at a party, and for one dangerous second remembers only the good parts. The road trip. The inside joke. The way they made coffee. Somehow the months of feeling small have gone blurry. Or it's an old job they hated, and now they catch themselves saying, the people were great, though. Memory is a generous editor: it keeps the flavor and cuts the cost. The Israelites, out of slavery and eating manna in the desert, do exactly this, and the Torah quotes their grocery list.
screen: `ONLY THE GOOD PARTS.` → `MEMORY, THE GENEROUS EDITOR.` → `A GROCERY LIST FROM EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Numbers eleven. The camp starts to crave. First the mixed crowd that came out of Egypt with them, then everyone, weeping in their tent doorways: "We remember the fish, which we were wont to eat in Egypt for nought; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic". Now, they say, our throats are dry, and there's nothing but this manna. You can almost smell the list. But look at two words: for nought. Free. The fish in Egypt were free? The rabbis didn't buy it. The Sifrei, and Rashi after it, ask: these people weren't even given straw for free to make their bricks. Who was handing them free fish? No, the rabbis say, free meant free of commandments, free of responsibility. In Egypt nobody asked anything of them but labor, and nobody expected them to choose. That's a kind of ease, and it's real. Freedom is heavier. And notice what the list leaves out. No whip. No quota of bricks. No baby boys thrown into the river. The craving doesn't lie about the cucumbers; it just forgets everything around them. The Torah doesn't mock them for missing food. Missing things is human. It just puts their own words on the record, so anyone reading later can hear what nostalgia does.

444.title: Beha'alotcha: seventy elders (Numbers 11:16–29)
444.hook: Moses shares the load and says "would that all the LORD's people were prophets"
444.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads the seventy elders as a root of shared leadership, and the Mishnah links the great court of seventy-one, the Sanhedrin, to Moses and the seventy; Moses' answer to Joshua is often quoted as a model of a leader without jealousy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people wept for Egypt's fish and forgot the whip. Your line was Egypt wasn't free. Today, what that complaint does to Moses.

Every office has one: the person who does everything. They answer every email, fix every crisis, carry the whole project in their head, until one afternoon they sit in the car in the parking lot and can't make themselves go in. Moses hits that wall in Numbers eleven. A whole people is weeping for meat at their tent doors, and he turns to God and says something close to: did I give birth to these people? Am I supposed to carry them like a nurse carries a baby? I can't do this alone. It's too heavy for me.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOES EVERYTHING.` → `I CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.` → `MOSES HITS THE WALL.`

segments.voice: God's answer isn't a pep talk. It's a reorganization. Gather seventy of the elders, God says. I'll take some of the spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they'll carry the burden of the people with you, so you don't carry it alone. Moses gathers them around the tent of meeting, the spirit rests on them, and they prophesy. But two men named on the list, Eldad and Medad, stayed back in the camp, and the spirit rests on them there too. They prophesy in the middle of the camp, outside the official circle. A young man runs to tell Moses. Joshua, Moses' loyal assistant, is alarmed: my lord Moses, stop them. Moses answers: are you jealous for my sake? "would that all the LORD'S people were prophets, that the LORD would put His spirit upon them!" Moses does two things here. He shares the load: seventy now carry what one was crushing under. And he shares the credit, more than shares it. Two unauthorized prophets in the camp aren't a threat to him; he wishes everyone had what they have. Later Jewish tradition saw the beginnings of the great court here: seventy elders plus Moses, seventy-one, the number of the Sanhedrin. But the line that lasts is Moses' wish. A leader who wants everyone to have the spirit isn't diminished by it. He's freed.

segments.voice: Look at what you carry alone that someone else could hold a corner of, a chore, a worry, the care of an aging parent, and name one person who could take it. 445.title: Beha'alotcha: five words (Numbers 12:13)
445.hook: Moses' prayer for Miriam is five Hebrew words: heal her now, O God
445.howItsDone: Moses' five-word prayer, El na r'fa na lah, is often quoted in Jewish prayer for the sick, and synagogues recite the Mi Shebeirach for healing with the names of those who are ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seventy elders shared Moses' load, and he wished the spirit on everyone. Your line was would all were prophets.

A hospital waiting room at three in the morning. Nobody there is giving speeches. People mutter please, please, or just a name, over and over. A father in a plastic chair whispers four or five words into his folded hands and then says nothing for an hour. Ask anyone who's sat in that room whether those words counted. Moses once stood in that kind of moment, for his own sister. His whole prayer was five words long.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PLEASE, PLEASE, A NAME.` → `FIVE WORDS FOR HIS SISTER.`

segments.voice: Numbers twelve. Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses, about the Cushite woman he married, and about something deeper: has God spoken only through Moses? Hasn't God spoken through us too? The Torah pauses to say that Moses was very humble, more than anyone on earth. Then God calls all three out to the tent, defends Moses, and leaves. And Miriam is struck with a skin affliction, white as snow. Aaron begs Moses. And Moses, who has just been criticized by her, cries out: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." In Hebrew: El na, r'fa na lah. Five words. No speech, no list of her merits, no bargaining. Just her, God, and now. The Talmud, in Berakhot, tells of a student leading prayer who went on and on, and the others complained. The teacher, Rabbi Eliezer, said: he's no longer than Moses, who prayed forty days and nights. Another student prayed very briefly, and they complained again. Rabbi Eliezer said: he's no shorter than Moses, who prayed El na, r'fa na lah. Both lengths count. Miriam is shut outside the camp for seven days, and the people don't move until she comes back. The Mishnah says why: once, Miriam waited by the river to watch over baby Moses. So a whole nation waited for her.

446.title: Shelach: go and see (Numbers 13:1–2)
446.hook: twelve scouts are sent to see the land
446.howItsDone: Shelach is read in synagogue in the yearly Torah cycle; the image of two scouts carrying a giant grape cluster on a pole is a familiar one in Jewish art, and the story of the scouts is studied as a lesson in how people see and report.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses prayed five words for Miriam, and a whole people waited for her. Your line was short prayers count. Today, a new portion, at the edge of the land.

Before you sign a lease, you visit the apartment. You open the closets, run the shower, check whether the windows face a brick wall. Before a big move, people drive through the new town at night to see if it's quiet. Nobody wants to commit to a place sight unseen. The Israelites are camped in the wilderness of Paran, at the edge of the promised land. The next step is to walk in. And first, someone wants a look around.
screen: `VISIT BEFORE YOU SIGN.` → `AT THE EDGE OF THE LAND.` → `FIRST, A LOOK AROUND.`

segments.voice: God says to Moses: "Send thou men, that they may spy out the land of Canaan". In Hebrew, shelach lecha: send for yourself. That extra word, lecha, caught Rashi's eye. He reads it as permission, not command: send if you want to; I'm not ordering it. Why put it that way? Because in Deuteronomy, Moses remembers that the people asked for it. They wanted a report first. So twelve men go, one leader from each tribe. One of them, Hoshea, gets a new name from Moses: Yehoshua, Joshua. Moses gives them a careful list of questions. See the land, what it is. The people living there: strong or weak, few or many. The cities: open camps or fortified. The soil: rich or poor. Are there trees? Be of good courage, he says, and bring back some of its fruit. It was the season of the first ripe grapes. They go for forty days, from the south to the far north. Past Hebron, in a valley later called Eshcol, cluster, they cut a single bunch of grapes so heavy that two men carry it between them on a pole. Pomegranates and figs too. The verb for their mission, latur, means to scout, to explore, to go around and look. Looking isn't the problem. Moses asked them to see, and to bring back something real. What they do with what they saw, as we'll find, is the test.

447.title: Shelach: as grasshoppers (Numbers 13:33)
447.hook: "we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight"
447.howItsDone: Teachers often take up the scouts' line about grasshoppers when Shelach is read; they use it, and the midrash on it, to talk about self-image, and about the difference between what we see and what we assume.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve scouts went to see the land and brought back a cluster of grapes. Your line was go and see. Today, they come back.

A candidate sits in the hallway before a job interview, already sure he's the least qualified person in the building. When he's called in, his shoulders drop. He talks too fast and apologizes before answering. The person across the desk, who had no opinion of him a minute ago, starts to form one, based on the one he walked in with. It isn't magic. People read how we hold ourselves. Twelve scouts come back from forty days in the land, carrying grapes, and ten of them deliver a report with a line people still quote.
screen: `SURE HE'S THE LEAST.` → `PEOPLE READ HOW WE HOLD OURSELVES.` → `TEN SCOUTS, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: The report starts out true. The land does flow with milk and honey, they say, and here's its fruit. Then comes the word but. The people there are strong; the cities are walled and very large. As the crowd grows uneasy, the report darkens. Ten of the scouts now say the land devours its inhabitants, and everyone there is huge. Then the line: there we saw the Nephilim, the giants, "and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight." Two halves. The first is honest: we felt tiny. The second is a guess dressed up as a fact. How could the scouts possibly know what the people of the land thought of them? A midrash imagines God catching exactly this: I don't mind that you felt like grasshoppers, but who told you how I made you look in their eyes? The Talmud gives the scouts a little evidence: they overheard the locals say there are ants in the vineyards that look like people. But the book of Joshua tells a different story. A woman in Jericho named Rahab tells two new spies that terror of Israel has fallen on her land, ever since they heard how the sea dried up before them. Their hearts melted. The people the scouts feared were afraid too. The scouts saw a fact, big people in walled cities, and let a feeling write the rest of the report. Their picture of themselves became the picture they gave everyone else.

segments.voice: Think of one situation coming up that makes you feel small, a meeting, a family dinner, a room full of people who seem bigger, and notice the picture of yourself you're already carrying in. 448.title: Shelach: another spirit (Numbers 14:24)
448.hook: Caleb "had another spirit with him" and trusted they could go up
448.howItsDone: Caleb and Joshua are remembered in Jewish teaching as the two scouts who trusted; the Talmud's account of Caleb praying alone at the patriarchs' graves in Hebron is often told with this portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scouts felt like grasshoppers and guessed everyone saw them that way. Your line was how you see yourself shows. Today, the scout who didn't.

The meeting's going badly. Someone has laid out every reason the plan will fail, and they're good reasons. Heads are nodding. The mood in the room is sliding toward no. Then one person, who saw the same numbers, clears their throat and says: actually, I think we can do this. It's not a comfortable moment. The room turns to look, and not all the looks are friendly. In Numbers thirteen, that person is named Caleb. He says it to a crowd that's about to cry all night.
screen: `EVERY REASON IT WILL FAIL.` → `THE ROOM SLIDES TOWARD NO.` → `ONE VOICE: WE CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Caleb, from the tribe of Judah, was one of the twelve scouts. He saw the same walls and the same giants. As the others' report spreads fear, he quiets the people: let's go up at once and take it; we can certainly do it. The ten answer: we can't; they're stronger than us. That night the whole people weeps. Then Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes in grief and plead: the land is very, very good. Don't rebel. Don't be afraid of its people; God is with us. The crowd's answer is to reach for stones. Then God speaks about Caleb: "But My servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed Me fully", he will enter the land. In Hebrew, ruach acheret: another spirit, a different spirit. Not different eyes; he saw what they saw. A different spirit about what he saw. The Talmud adds a detail from the scouting trip itself. One verse says they went up into the south and he came to Hebron, singular. Who's he? The rabbis say it was Caleb, alone, going to Hebron to pray at the graves of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, asking to be saved from the scouts' plan. In that telling, the different spirit came with work and prayer, and a willingness to stand apart from his own group. And it lasts. In the book of Joshua, Caleb, now eighty-five, says he's as strong as the day he scouted, and asks for Hebron, giants and all.
screen: `SAME WALLS, SAME GIANTS.` · `LET'S GO UP AT ONCE.` · `RUACH ACHERET: ANOTHER SPIRIT.` · `ALONE TO HEBRON, TO PRAY.` · then, large: `A DIFFERENT SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where the mood has slid toward no, a family plan, a team project, a friend who's given up on something, and look honestly at the walls and the giants; Caleb did. Then ask what a different spirit would see in the same facts, and find one true sentence that begins, we can.
Shelach. This week: second chances exist, Egypt wasn't free, would all were prophets, short prayers count, go and see, how you see yourself shows, and now Caleb's different spirit.
Your line: a different spirit. Same walls, same giants, another way of seeing them. Day four hundred forty-eight, done.
